item.title: Olfactory network variability is associated with odor identification and cognitive performance in mild cognitive impairment.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundOdor identification impairment is an early marker of Alzheimer's disease pathology and predicts dementia conversion in mild cognitive impairment (MCI). However, the pathophysiological role of dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) variability within olfactory networks remains unclear.ObjectiveTo characterize seed-based dFC variability across olfactory pathways in MCI with odor identification impairment (MCI-OII) and examine its associations with olfactory and cognitive performance.MethodsNinety-seven patients with MCI were recruited and subdivided into MCI-OII and those without odor identification impairment (MCI-NOII), along with 97 age-matched healthy controls (HC). All participants underwent neuropsychological assessment, olfactory testing, and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Seed-based dFC variability was computed using a sliding window approach. Correlation and exploratory mediation analyses examined associations among abnormal dFC, odor identification, and cognition.ResultsCompared to MCI-NOII and HC, MCI-OII exhibited increased dFC variability between the left piriform cortex/right insula and right caudate nucleus, and between the left insula and left middle frontal gyrus. For the connection between the left insula and left cerebellar lobule VI, dFC variability showed a graded pattern from MCI-OII to HC to MCI-NOII. Increased caudate-centered dFC variability was associated with poorer odor identification, memory, and executive performance. Furthermore, exploratory mediation analyses suggested indirect associations involving odor identification, caudate-centered dFC variability, and memory or executive function.ConclusionsMCI-OII is characterized by increased olfactory-network dFC variability, particularly in caudate-centered pathways. These findings suggest that dFC variability may serve as a candidate network-level marker of concurrent olfactory impairment and cognitive dysfunction in MCI.

item.title: The extended default mode network dysconnectivity in schizophrenia
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The default mode network (DMN) extends beyond cortex into subcortical structures, yet how this extended DMN (eDMN) is causally reorganized in schizophrenia (SZ) remains unclear. Here, resting-state fMRI from 74 healthy controls (HC) and 66 SZ patients was analyzed. Subject-specific eDMNs were identified using spatially-constrained independent component analysis, and effective connectivity among 13 regions was estimated with spectral dynamic causal modeling, with group effects assessed using parametric empirical Bayes. Causal centrality—a dynamics-sensitive and causality-based measure of nodal importance—was computed per region, compared between groups, and correlated with MATRICS cognitive scores in patients. Causal centrality rankings were highly similar across groups (ρ = 0.87), with both favoring subcortical over cortical regions. Group differences were regionally specific: temporal cortex was more causally central in patients, whereas posterior parietal cortex was more causally central in controls. Most connection-level SZ-HC differences originated from ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, prefrontal cortex, basal forebrain, temporal cortex, and thalamus. In patients, temporal causal centrality correlated negatively with reasoning/problem-solving, and ventrolateral prefrontal causal centrality with processing speed and composite cognition. The eDMN's core causal architecture is preserved in schizophrenia, but temporal influence is enhanced and parietal influence attenuated—alterations that are behaviorally meaningful and consistent with pathological reorganization.

item.title: DECODE: DEcomposition of COupled and DEcoupled Brain States: Separating Structure-Coupled and Structure-Decoupled Functional Organization in Alzheimers Disease
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Brain functional activity emerges within an underlying structural scaffold. While structural network connectivity provides a relatively stable anatomical backbone for large-scale communication, functional interactions are high-dimensional and temporally dynamic, forming recurrent patterns that can be represented in a latent space of transient functional states. Yet, how these transient functional states are organized and the extent to which they remain constrained by structural network connectivity or become relatively decoupled from structural organization over time remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we introduce DECODE (DEcomposition of COupled and DEcoupled Brain States), a data-driven latent-space framework that uses independent component analysis (ICA) and multimodal data to decompose resting-state dynamic functional network connectivity into a lower-dimensional representation of transient functional states. These states capture temporally varying structure-coupled and structure-decoupled patterns using diffusion MRI-derived structural network connectivity priors. Structure-coupled states reflect functional configurations more strongly anchored to major structural motifs, whereas structure-decoupled states represent configurations less constrained by the identified structural organization, while potentially remaining within structurally defined dynamical bounds. DECODE identifies reproducible structure-coupled and structure-decoupled states, with mean squared error reconstruction of dynamic information < 0.1 and adjusted R-squared = 0.4. Applied to Alzheimers disease (AD), DECODE revealed stronger group differences (FDR-corrected p-value 0.05) in both connectivity organization and temporal dynamics for decoupled states. These findings suggest that functional states less constrained by identified structural organization may be more vulnerable to AD-related disruption, whereas structure-coupled states may be relatively preserved. More broadly, DECODE provides a reproducible and generalizable framework for quantifying how functional dynamics are shaped by, or diverge from, structural organization by incorporating a latent representation of the structural connectome as an informative prior. Our findings established structural and functional alignment variation by distinguishing dynamic functional patterns closely coupled with structure from those that deviate from it.

item.title: Allometric scaling of resting-state EEG network topography across childhood and adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Brain network topography undergoes complex reorganization throughout childhood and adolescence. Quantifying the functional form of this maturation remains a key challenge. Here, we applied developmental allometry to sensor-level resting-state EEG networks from 1,957 participants aged 5–21 years (Healthy Brain Network). We fitted power laws of age to four graph-theoretic indices (small-worldness, global and local efficiency, modularity) across five frequency bands. Nineteen of the 20 band-by-index exponents were negative. Low-frequency (delta and theta) small-worldness showed the steepest declines (alpha = -0.878 and − 0.868), indicating a near-halving of the metric with each doubling of age. Lobe-resolved analyses revealed a pan-lobar but non-uniform decline, with posterior regions showing steeper age-related changes than frontal regions in specific bands. While raw-space cross-validation did not uniquely favor the power law over linear models, its scale-free exponent provides a unified parameter to compare developmental rates across spatial and spectral scales. Individual deviations from this topology did not track dimensional psychopathology. These exponents provide a quantitative reference for EEG network topography maturation and highlight the necessity of frequency- and region-specific modeling.

item.title: A realistic model of resting-state BOLD spectra in white matter
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Resting-state BOLD signals in white matter show a spectral elevation near 0.06 Hz on an exponentially decaying background, and white-matter hemodynamic response functions (HRFs) have a prominent initial dip. We model the resting signal as shot noise: randomly timed neural events are filtered by the HRF, so that the spectrum is the input spectrum multiplied by the squared HRF gain, plus instrumental noise. The initial dip and post-stimulus undershoot remove low-frequency power, making the white-matter HRF a band-pass filter with maximum gain near 0.05 Hz. One set of physiological parameters fits both a measured white-matter HRF (R² = 0.993) and the group-mean white-matter spectrum (R² = 0.987), with a resting transit time of about 4 s and a metabolic response weighted about twice as heavily as in gray matter. Deepening the dip raises the filter gain and moves its maximum toward 0.06 Hz, linking the dip to the spectral feature. A narrower line in individual spectra is reproduced either by an underdamped HRF that matches the measured response over its first 20 s or by a rhythmic input near 0.06 Hz. The model identifies which HRF properties could explain the decline of the peak with age.

item.title: Spontaneous Neuronal Activity in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Insights from Human and Animal Studies.
item.description:
The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
Developmental spontaneous neuronal activity (SNA) plays an instrumental role in the generation of precise brain circuits. Spontaneous activity patterns guide neuronal differentiation, synaptic refinement, and circuit formation; consequently, perturbations in these activity patterns can profoundly influence brain network organization. Growing evidence suggests that mutations in autism-associated genes lead to alterations of the SNA pattern during early brain development, thereby giving rise to the behavioral features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This review integrates findings from neuroimaging studies, which reveal widespread alterations in neuronal excitability in individuals with ASD. Regional homogeneity and functional connectivity analyses consistently demonstrate region-specific abnormalities, including hyperactivity in higher-order cortical regions, hypoactivity in sensorimotor areas, and disrupted long-range connectivity. These functional alterations are closely linked to the underlying molecular and cellular mechanisms such as excitation-inhibition (E/I) imbalance, impaired GABAergic signaling, glutamatergic dysregulation, and abnormalities in calcium-dependent signaling pathways. Identification of activity-based biomarkers, together with advanced neuroimaging techniques and computational and machine learning (ML) approaches, may facilitate early diagnosis of ASD. Understanding the origin and consequences of alterations in SNA provides a unifying framework for identifying novel targets for designing pharmacological intervention strategies.

item.title: Dynamic Brain Network Transitions and Sensorimotor Performance Across the Adult Lifespan.
item.description:
Seminars in ultrasound, CT, and MR
Healthy adult aging is accompanied by subtle variations in fine sensorimotor control and cognitive flexibility. Traditional static neuroimaging approaches often overlook short-term temporal dynamics. This study investigated cross-sectional associations between temporal brain state transitions and sensorimotor performance-specifically force matching and motor learning adaptation-across the adult lifespan. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) and behavioral data from 218 healthy adults (aged 18-88 years; 99 females, 119 males) were analyzed across three age groups: young (18-35 years; n = 45; 25 females, 20 males), middle-aged (>35-60 years; n = 88; 37 females, 51 males), and older adults (>60 years; n = 85; 37 females, 48 males).Sex distribution did not differ significantly across age groups (p = 0.302). Time varying functional connectivity was modeled to extract Fractional Occupancy (FO), Mean Dwell Time (MDT), and global Switching Rate (SR) across six recurrent brain states. Behavioral metrics included finger force overcompensation (force matching) and spatial trajectory error during late-exposure motor learning. Advancing age was significantly associated with higher trajectory error during motor learning (p < 0.001) and greater force overcompensation (p ≤ 0.001). Post-hoc comparisons revealed non-linear cross-sectional differences, with older adults exhibiting higher error margins than young and middle-aged groups. Global switching rate (SR) demonstrated a statistically significant inverse association with motor learning error (β = -0.122 to -0.280, p < 0.03), indicating that higher dynamic network flexibility is associated with lower motor adaptation error. Furthermore, age was negatively correlated with switching rate (β = -0.166, p = 0.023). In the Executive Control Network (State 3), females exhibited significantly higher FO (p = 0.003) and adjusted MDT (p = 0.007) compared to males. Additionally, older males showed a nominal positive association with Task-Positive Network (State 5) dwell time (ρ = 0.204, p = 0.026). These findings suggest an age-associated pattern of "dynamic rigidity," characterized by a reduced propensity for global brain state switching within cross-sectional observations. Fluid state transition capacity-rather than isolated state occupancy-offers significant explanatory relevance for sensorimotor adaptation across the adult lifespan.

item.title: High cortical lesion burden moderates the association between brain networks and processing speed in older adults with multiple sclerosis.
item.description:
Brain imaging and behavior
Cortical lesions (CL) are common in older adults with multiple sclerosis (OAMS), but their influence on the relationship between resting-state network strength (RSNS) and cognitive function in OAMS remains underexplored. This study aimed to determine whether CL moderates associations between RSNS and processing speed in OAMS. 82 OAMS participants (mean age: 64.4 ± 4.1 years; males/females: 26/56) were scanned in a 3T scanner. Identification of CL on double inversion-recovery (DIR) MRI images in this study was performed using established consensus recommendations. We estimated functional brain networks using a data-driven procedure to extract seven intrinsic resting-state networks. The Symbol-Digit-Modalities Test (SDMT), an established test of processing speed and working memory, served as the cognitive outcome measure. Multiple linear regressions, adjusted for sociodemographic covariates, examined the relationship between RSNS and SDMT performance with CL (three levels: no CL, 1-2 CL, and ≥ 3 CL) as a moderator. Significant CL-by-network interactions in models adjusted for sociodemographic covariates and white matter lesion load indicated that high-burden CL vs. no CL moderated the association between RSNS and SDMT in the auditory network (AUD) (p = 0.030), dorsal attention network (DAN) (p = 0.033), left frontoparietal network (LFPN) (p = 0.030), and posterior DMN (pDMN) (p = 0.030). Conditional effects showed that high-burden CLs attenuated positive associations between specific brain networks and SDMT performance. These findings suggest that higher CL burden restricts the functional brain support for processing speed and working memory performance in OAMS.

item.title: Beyond sleep macrostructure: a high-definition review of acupuncture's electrophysiological signatures in modulating sleep microarchitecture (spectral power, spindles, and slow oscillations).
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Sleep science has shifted from coarse stage-based metrics toward a microstructural perspective that treats electroencephalographic biomarkers, spectral power, sleep spindles, and slow oscillations as candidate windows onto restorative brain function. This high-definition review evaluates whether acupuncture has been shown to modify these features. Direct evidence from natural overnight sleep is currently very limited: most available electrophysiological studies were conducted during quiet wakefulness, in resting daytime EEG recordings from clinical groups, or under propofol anesthesia. These studies demonstrate that acupuncture or related electrical acupoint stimulation can produce state-, region-, and frequency-dependent changes in EEG power and network organization, but they do not yet establish increased NREM spindle density, improved slow-oscillation-spindle coupling, enhanced slow-wave morphology, memory consolidation, or glymphatic clearance. We therefore distinguish directly observed findings from indirect mechanistic support and from hypotheses that require prospective testing. Plausible pathways include ascending somatosensory influences on thalamocortical excitability, autonomic and hypothalamic effects that may reduce hyperarousal, and peripheral or central neurochemical processes involving adenosine, GABA, serotonin, and BDNF; however, the causal sequence from needling to sleep microarchitecture remains unproven. Future progress requires preregistered, adequately powered, multi-night studies using validated spindle and slow-wave detectors, explicit control estimands, and multimodal measurements. Biomarker-guided and closed-loop acupuncture should presently be regarded as a research framework rather than an established treatment strategy.

item.title: Tau-vulnerable medial temporal lobe connectivity drives a functional-to-synaptic cascade in Alzheimer's disease
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Distinct tau-vulnerable and relatively spared subregions exist within the medial temporal lobe (MTL). However, it remains unclear that how functional connectivity (FC), anchored to tau-vulnerable MTL subregions, is related to tau pathology, synaptic dysfunction, and cognitive decline across the Alzheimer's disease (AD) continuum. We here probe into this with resting-state fMRI data from a discovery cohort (ADNI; N = 386; cognitively normal [CN], mild cognitive impairment [MCI], and AD; 144 with 2-year follow-up) and an independent validation cohort at local hospital (N = 100; CN, subjective cognitive decline [SCD], and MCI; 25 receiving high-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation [HF-rTMS]). We first separated the MTL into subregions with high and low neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) burden based on histological atlases, and calculated the seed-based whole-brain FC for each subregion. Second, group differences were assessed using ANCOVA, and associations with amyloid-β (Aβ)/tau pathology, synaptic biomarkers, and cognitive performance were examined. Third, serial mediation, cross-lagged, and longitudinal regression analyses were performed to investigate the proposed pathological sequence, with additional evidence from HF-rTMS intervention and autopsy-confirmed Braak staging. Our results showed that, with the development of AD, FC reductions were focused on the high-NFT MTL network, particularly involving the inferior temporal gyrus and precuneus. Baseline tau burden in high-NFT MTL regions was able to predict subsequent FC alterations. Interestingly, FC between the high-NFT MTL and global brain showed region-specific associations with synaptic biomarkers, including negative associations in the cerebellum and positive associations in the precentral gyrus. We also observed a divergent association between the FC and cognition or pathology at different AD stages, shifting from positive in the early stages to negative in advanced AD. Serial mediation analyses supported a pathway linking tau burden to cognitive impairment through altered high-NFT MTL connectivity in the precuneus and occipital regions and subsequent synaptic dysfunction. Cross-lagged and longitudinal analyses further confirmed the proposed temporal sequence. Furthermore, HF-rTMS-related cognitive improvements were partially associated with enhanced synaptic plasticity through changes in precuneus-high-NFT MTL connectivity. Collectively, these findings support a spatiotemporal framework linking the dysfunction of tau-vulnerable MTL network to synaptic impairment and cognitive decline, highlighting high-NFT MTL-based FC as a potential imaging marker tracking AD progression.

item.title: Exploring subacute effects of a DMT and harmine meditation retreat on the brain's control energy landscape
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Modeling the brain as a controllable structural network allows the estimation of the control energy (CE) required to reach functional states, where low-CE states are more accessible. Psychedelics are thought to acutely flatten the brain's CE landscape, broadening the repertoire of reachable states, but whether this reorganization persists into the subacute ``afterglow" window is largely unknown. This exploratory study uses rs-fMRI from a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (N = 39; 19 verum [N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT) + harmine, Ayahuasca-inspired formulation], 20 placebo) scanned before and after a three-day meditation retreat. We compute CE on a group human connectome project (HCP) structural connectome under two approaches that emphasize long and short timescale dynamics. Globally, we found no systematic shift in the distribution of CE between transitions, however mean CE increased in both groups at the long timescale approach. Surviving network effects emerge when a network's intrinsic timescale matches the stabilization regime. In the long timescale regime, the central executive network (CEN) showed an increase in post-retreat CE within the verum group that survived Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR-BH) correction. Although CE and functional connectivity are distinct, this higher CEN cost may relate to the reduced within-network connectivity previously reported subacutely after psilocybin. The default mode network (DMN) also showed a post-retreat CE increase in both groups, but neither change survived FDR correction. In the short timescale approach, the visual network (VN) showed a FDR-BH CE decrease within the verum group, consistent with reduced dynamical demand in a region acutely engaged by DMT. To examine whether changes were concentrated in less accessible states, we additionally analyzed rare brain states, defined by the top decile of information content. This analysis revealed a modest session × condition interaction in the long timescale approach. Overall, the two timescale lenses surface different network effects, that align with cortical timescale hierarchies. These findings point to network- and timescale-specific, rather than global, CE changes in the afterglow window, though effects are small and heterogeneous and require confirmation in larger samples. Characterizing whether and where psychedelic effects persist into the subacute window is relevant to psychedelic-assisted therapy, including safety, therapeutic timing, and durability of drug effects. More broadly, considering cortical timescale hierarchies may help identify network-specific CE changes that might be less apparent when networks are evaluated under a single dynamical timescale.

item.title: FDTest: Fluctuation-dissipation theorem as a test for memory effects in brain dynamics.
item.description:
PLoS computational biology
A central challenge in neuroscience is to understand how the brain flexibly balances local and distributed information processing to support diverse cognitive and conscious states. We hypothesize that a key signature of this balance is the presence of memory effects, which arise when a brain region's future activity depends not only on its current state, but also on past information fed back from the wider network. Here we introduce the FDTest, a method for assessing local memory effects in multidimensional systems by measuring violations of a generalized Fluctuation-dissipation theorem (FDT). We first apply this framework to whole-brain models fitted to human neuroimaging data, demonstrating that the brain's memory structure reflects its underlying connectivity. We then extend the analysis to individualized models of subjects during wakefulness and deep sleep. Memory effects are consistently stronger in wakefulness, indicating richer inter-regional dependencies and more integrated dynamics. These findings establish local memory as a dynamical marker of brain state and position the FDTest as a principled tool for probing the hidden structure of neural dynamics.

item.title: Posterior-lateral basal forebrain cholinergic nuclei hypoconnectivity in the inferior frontal cortex is associated with verbal fluency deficits in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Schizophrenia (Heidelberg, Germany)
Cognitive impairment is a core feature of schizophrenia and remains insufficiently addressed by current treatments. Increasing evidence implicates the cholinergic system, particularly the basal forebrain cholinergic nuclei (BFCN), in cognitive dysfunction. While structural alterations of the BFCN have been reported, alterations in their intrinsic functional connectivity (iFC) remain unclear. The present study examined the iFC of anterior and posterior BFCN subdivisions (aBFCN, pBFCN) in schizophrenia and tested associations with cognitive performance. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from the COBRE dataset were analyzed, including 73 healthy controls (HC) and 51 patients with schizophrenia (SCZ). Seed-based connectivity analyses were performed for aBFCN and pBFCN. Group differences were assessed voxel-wise, and group-dependent associations with phonemic verbal fluency (FAS) and processing speed (BACS-SC) were tested using hierarchical regression controlling for age, sex, IQ, and smoking status; verbal learning and memory (HVLT) was examined as a specificity analysis. Exploratory molecular mapping used normative PET-derived neurotransmitter maps, supplemented by spatial-autocorrelation-preserving null models. Distinct connectivity patterns of aBFCN and pBFCN were observed, consistent with previous reports in HC. Compared with HC, SCZ showed reduced pBFCN connectivity with a cluster in the right inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis; BA44; p = 0.018, FWE-corrected), whereas no significant differences were observed for aBFCN. The Group × pBFCN-IFG connectivity interaction was significant for FAS (p = 0.014) but not BACS-SC (p = 0.762) or HVLT (p = 0.514). In SCZ, higher pBFCN-IFG connectivity was associated with better FAS performance. Descriptive molecular mapping showed above-average representation of M1 and α4β2 receptor maps as well as several non-cholinergic targets; however, no molecular target showed significant spatial correspondence after spatial-autocorrelation-aware testing and FDR correction. These findings provide evidence for selective pBFCN hypoconnectivity with the right inferior frontal gyrus in schizophrenia. Its association with verbal fluency suggests that disrupted pBFCN connectivity with the inferior frontal cortex may contribute to altered executive control processes involved in verbal fluency in schizophrenia. Together, these findings extend previous evidence of BFCN abnormalities in schizophrenia by demonstrating a systems-level functional alteration of pBFCN-cortical connectivity and its relationship with cognitive performance.

item.title: Spontaneously emerging patterns show category-biased similarity to task-evoked visual patterns beyond human visual cortex.
item.description:
NeuroImage
In the absence of any task, spontaneous brain activity exhibits patterns that resemble those evoked by natural stimuli and behaviors. This raises the possibility that resting-state activity patterns may relate to maintenance and consolidation of behaviorally relevant information states. Using functional MRI (fMRI) data from 100 healthy adults in the Human Connectome Project, we investigated whether neural signals evoked by specific visual stimuli (body parts, faces, places, tools) show similarity to resting-state activity across non-canonical visual areas, i.e., motor and association cortices. Participants underwent a working memory task and resting-state scanning. We analyzed multivoxel pattern similarity between task-evoked activations and spontaneous activity in bilateral hand motor regions and attention-related networks. Spatial correlations between task-evoked multivoxel patterns for each visual category and frame-by-frame resting-state signals were computed, with the upper 90% distribution percentile (U90) as a similarity metric. We found that resting-state patterns in the left hemisphere hand motor region showed significantly higher similarity to tool-evoked patterns than place-evoked patterns, consistent with the interpretation that tools recruit motor affordances and hand‑object associations in motor cortex. In the bilateral dorsal attention network, resting-task similarity for non-face evoked patterns significantly exceeded that for faces. Moreover, effects localized to posterior dorsal attention network, aligning with the dorsal visual pathway's role in spatial-action coding of behaviorally relevant objects. These results suggest that resting-state activity in non-visual cortices shows category-biased similarity to task-evoked visual patterns, consistent with the view that spontaneous neural dynamics preferentially reactivate ecologically salient stimuli.

item.title: Altered dynamic brain states and potential transcriptomic correlates in autism spectrum disorder.
item.description:
Brain imaging and behavior
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is associated with widespread alterations in functional brain networks, but its transient dynamic brain states and potential transcriptomic correlates remain unclear. We applied Leading Eigenvector Dynamics Analysis (LEiDA) to resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 110 individuals with ASD and 110 healthy controls (HCs) from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange I (ABIDE I) dataset. Five recurrent phase-locking states were identified, and dynamic brain state metrics were compared between groups. Compared with HCs, individuals with ASD showed reduced fractional occupancy (FO) of State 5, which was predominantly characterized by the visual network with additional involvement of the sensorimotor network. Exploratory analyses within the ASD group revealed nominal negative associations between State 4 FO and ADOS total and social scores. To investigate potential transcriptomic correlates, we derived an ROI-wise ASD-HC State 5 weighted beta map and related it to Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA) gene expression data and SFARI ASD risk gene sets. SFARI ASD risk gene sets showed a consistent pattern of negative spatial associations with the ASD-related State 5 imaging phenotype, but these associations did not reach statistical significance after BrainSMASH testing and FDR correction. Exploratory rank-based Gene Ontology (GO) analysis implicated biological functions related to neuronal structure, synaptic function, and the regulation of neuronal excitability. These findings identify alterations in dynamic brain state organization in ASD and provide exploratory transcriptomic clues to their potential biological context.

item.title: Individual differences in eating attitudes are associated with distinct resting-state functional connectivity patterns in healthy adults.
item.description:
Brain imaging and behavior
Eating disorders (EDs) and obesity are multifaceted conditions that reflect extremes of over- and under-nutrition and may cause significant life-altering complications. The individual susceptibility to potential development of EDs or obesity is determined by specific eating behaviors and attitudes toward food. Whether this behavioural vulnerability is also associated with specific neural connectivity patterns is unknown. This study aimed to investigate associations between resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) and nonpathological premorbid attitudes toward food in healthy adults. Forty-eight healthy adults (mean age = 61.79 ± 11.07) underwent structural and functional MRI acquisitions on a 3-T MRI scanner. Attitudes toward food and eating were assessed using the Adult Eating Behavior Questionnaire (AEBQ). The relationship between seed-based connectivity and appetitive traits derived from the AEBQ was examined with general linear model group-level inferences, focusing on brain regions involved in behavioural control and salience processing. Overeating susceptibility was associated with stronger rs-FC between the right inferior frontal gyrus and the posterior cingulate/precuneus, as well as greater coupling between limbic/peri-limbic areas and reward-salience as well as prefrontal-control regions. In contrast, undereating vulnerability was associated with enhanced connectivity between right hippocampus and left opercular-insular regions. Finally, food fussiness was associated with the coupling between bilateral superior-frontal and prefrontal regions. Our findings suggest that increased rs-FC, specifically between regions involved in executive control, decision making, salience, reward evaluation and self-referential processing, predict attitudes toward food and eating that may increase individual susceptibility to EDs and obesity in healthy adults.

item.title: Capturing continuous spectrotemporal pupil—brain coupling with simultaneous wearable EEG/Eye tracking
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Spontaneous fluctuations in pupil diameter are closely linked to neural dynamics, yet most evidence for pupil—brain coupling has been obtained in conventional laboratory settings. We therefore asked whether the spectrotemporal and directional organization of such coupling can be captured with wearable systems to test their use in naturalistic settings. Using combined lightweight mobile EEG (MUSE) and eye tracking (Tobii Pro Glasses 3) devices, we investigated resting–state pupil—brain coupling and explored interoceptive attention to determine whether the core organizational principles observed with stationary equipment are detectable within and preserved across continuous recording states. Cross–correlation, mutual information, and Granger causality analyses revealed that pupil—brain coupling displayed clear frequency–dependent organization. Lower EEG frequencies (2–12Hz) preceded pupil dynamics by roughly 764ms, while higher frequencies showed a distinct coupling range. Granger–causality analysis further indicated predominantly EEG–to–pupil directional coupling. Similar observations were made during interoception. Overall, these findings align well and extend previous evidence on spontaneous pupil—brain coupling, demonstrating that lightweight and movable wearable devices are suitable to characterize spectrotemporal and directional pupil—brain interactions. In turn, these results encourage future fundamental and translational research in naturalistic environments.

item.title: Widespread oscillatory suppression in autism persists in the absence of psychotropic medication.
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Purpose: Investigate the neural oscillatory activity associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) using electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings in children and adolescents. Compare the corresponding oscillatory power between ASD patients taking psychotropic medication with a drug-naive group. Methods: ASD diagnosis was done using DSM-IV and CARS (Childhood Autism Rating Scale). EEG recordings employed 22 scalp electrodes (10/20 system). ASD vs. neurotypical groups were matched for sex and age (5 females; average age: ~10 years old). We analyzed the resting state (eyes open) EEG power spectrum during ~2-minute recordings. The multitaper FFT method was used to estimate spectral power for the delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma frequency bands. We pooled together data from several electrodes to compute comprehensive power spectra and assess the oscillatory behavior of macro brain regions. Results: We observed widespread (~4Hz - 20Hz) oscillatory suppression comprising the theta, alpha and beta frequency bands. The most widespread and robust ASD-associated power suppression was in the high theta and alpha bands. Delta and gamma bands showed no significant power change for any of the brain regions studied. Results from a subgroup of patients (N = 9) who never used psychotropics confirmed these findings, indicating that they are not an artifact of medication. Conclusion: Suppression in theta, alpha and beta oscillations may offer insights into the neurophysiological underpinnings of autism and could be used as an accessible and comprehensive tool in ASD diagnosis, regardless of the patients being or not on medication.

item.title: Neuroinflammation and Brain Network Remodeling in Alzheimer's Disease: Integrating DTI, fMRI, TSPO-PET, and Fluid Biomarkers.
item.description:
Current Alzheimer research
In Alzheimer's disease (AD), how neuroinflammation triggers white-matter injury and remodels functional networks remains a core unresolved question. This narrative review surveys research progress, technical approaches, and outstanding challenges of multimodal neuroimagingincluding diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), functional MRI (fMRI), translocator protein PET (TSPOPET), and fluid biomarkers-in elucidating neuroinflammation in AD. Five themes are discussed: molecular and fluid biomarkers of neuroinflammation; DTI-characterized signatures of white matter damage; fMRI-demonstrated functional network reorganization; alterations in structure-function coupling; and machine learning-enhanced multimodal data fusion strategies. Future multicenter longitudinal studies with standardized acquisition and analysis protocols are needed to dissect the causal chain of "inflammation → microstructural injury → network collapse → cognitive decline" and to establish an integrated imaging-biology framework for early screening and longitudinal monitoring of AD.

item.title: Hippocampal event updating and narrative relation-map updating during naturalistic memory encoding and retrieval
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Naturalistic memory depends on whether an event can be recalled and how accurately its original memory state is reinstated during successful recall. However, how brain-state changes around event transitions and changes in story relationships relate to these aspects of memory remains unclear. Here, we analysed functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 24 participants who viewed and freely recalled 43 naturalistic narrative events, measuring post-boundary hippocampal state changes and changes in narrative relationships. We found that larger late hippocampal state changes predicted successful event recall, with the effect confined to a specific post-boundary window. Among successfully recalled events, larger changes in narrative relationships were associated with more accurate reinstatement of hippocampal states. The relative associations of the two types of change also differed between memory outcomes. These findings suggest that brain-state updating and narrative-relation updating provide complementary perspectives on memory formation and reinstatement under naturalistic conditions.

item.title: Periodic theta and spectral–memory relationships differentiate amnestic mild cognitive impairment from healthy aging
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract BACKGROUND Amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI) carries an elevated risk of progression to Alzheimer's disease, yet no reliable resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) signature has separated it from healthy aging. Disease-related information may lie in spectral power itself, in how spectral activity relates to cognition, or in both. Standard analyses also conflate oscillatory changes with aperiodic background activity. METHODS In this cross-sectional study, we combined sensor- and individualized source-level analyses with spectral parameterization of high-density resting-state EEG from 150 participants (34 aMCI patients, 58 healthy older adults, 58 healthy younger adults) and tested how oscillatory activity related to memory within memory-network regions. RESULTS Both older groups showed higher beta and gamma power and flatter aperiodic slopes relative to younger adults, consistent with known aging effects. The clearest distinction between aMCI and healthy aging was in periodic theta. Patients showed higher theta than healthy older adults and resembled younger adults, an effect standard spectral analyses missed. Source-level gamma and beta power was associated with worse memory in aMCI but not healthy older adults, though only the precuneus beta difference was confirmed between groups. Age was more closely associated with slope flattening in patients than in healthy older adults. CONCLUSION These findings suggest that aMCI is distinguished from healthy aging not by the magnitude of spectral change, which the groups largely shared, but by specific alterations in oscillatory activity and its link to cognition. Elevated periodic theta and the altered precuneus beta–memory relationship stood out most and are promising markers for longitudinal work.

item.title: Increased Temporal Persistence of Reference-Invariant Frontopolar EEG Difference Amplitude in Autism Spectrum Disorder
item.description:
[预印本] Preprints.org
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has been associated with altered spectral activity and functional connectivity, but the temporal organization of bilateral EEG difference states remains poorly understood. We investigated whether the amplitude of the voltage difference between homologous scalp electrodes exhibits altered temporal persistence in ASD and whether this phenotype remains detectable after controlling for conventional EEG measures and putative ocular artifacts. Resting-state EEG from 129 children aged 8–13 years (63 ASD, 40 typically developing [TD], and 26 unaffected siblings [SIB]) was analyzed. Reference-invariant bilateral voltage differences were constructed across 23 homologous electrode pairs and four frequency bands, and persistence was quantified from lagged regression of their band-limited log-amplitude trajectories. Fp1–Fp2 delta-band persistence was the only target surviving false-discovery-rate correction across 92 comparisons. Persistence was greater in ASD than TD participants (0.673 ± 0.046 vs. 0.638 ± 0.041; Cohen’s d = 0.794; q = 0.0382), with differences concentrated at 50–400 ms. The phenotype showed repeated-run reliability (Spearman–Brown = 0.809), an ordered TD–SIB–ASD distribution, and associations with ASD beyond local persistence, spectral power, coherence, and weighted phase-lag index. In 99 participants (59 ASD, 40 TD), the adjusted group difference remained after conservative ICA-based removal of 40 putative ocular components (β = 0.03353, p = 0.000285) and broader removal of 58 components (β = 0.03231, p = 0.000440). The association also persisted after full-scale IQ adjustment and in male-only analyses. Although independently identified electrooculographic signals were unavailable, these results demonstrate robustness to the tested EEG-derived ocular-component removal procedures. Bilateral mismatch-amplitude persistence thus represents a complementary temporal EEG phenotype associated with ASD, distinct from the conventional spectral and connectivity measures examined.

item.title: Remembered Event Features Shape Default Mode Network Engagement during Emotional Memory Recall.
item.description:
eNeuro
Episodic memory involves reconstruction of past events through integration of multiple types of information, including perceptual details, narrative content, and emotional tone. The default mode network (DMN) is a set of regions thought to support episodic retrieval, yet it remains unclear how distinct subnetworks contribute to recall of these different memory features. Here, we examined how DMN subnetworks support and represent memory for naturalistic emotional events. Male and female human participants encoded short news videos that varied in emotional valence and recalled them in response to neutral cues during functional MRI scanning. Videos were again recalled 1 d later and memories were scored for perceptual and narrative details. Activity in the dorsomedial subnetwork was related to the emotional valence of the memory, while activity in the medial temporal subnetwork was associated with the number of perceptual details recalled. Multivariate pattern analyses further revealed that the medial temporal subnetwork exhibited greater pattern stability across recalls when recalling more perceptual details, while stability in the dorsomedial and core subnetworks was tied to emotional remembering. Our findings suggest that the dorsomedial subnetwork provides an affective frame for a memory, while the medial temporal subnetwork contributes perceptual specificity. These results demonstrate that the contents of memory retrieval shape network engagement during emotional recall, providing insight into how the brain reconstructs complex real-world experiences.

item.title: Evaluation of Brain Activity in Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder Using Standardized Low Resolution Electromagnetic Tomographic Analyses (sLORETA).
item.description:
Clinical EEG and neuroscience
This study evaluated Default Mode Network (DMN) brain activity in females with Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD)/Dysphoric PMS and asymptomatic controls using archival quantitative electroencephalography (qEEG) and standardized low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (sLORETA) data. Eyes-closed resting-state EEG analyses were examined across follicular and luteal menstrual cycle phases. The analytic sample included 157 participants: PMDD/Dysphoric PMS (n = 87) and asymptomatic controls (n = 70). Nonparametric Wilcoxon Signed Rank Tests were used for follicular-to-luteal within-group comparisons, and Mood's Median Test was used for luteal-phase between-group analyses. Asymptomatic controls showed significant follicular-to-luteal mean-Z changes in cingulate gyrus delta, cingulate gyrus theta, and insula theta. PMDD/Dysphoric PMS participants showed a significant percentage-of-aberrant-voxels change in angular gyrus beta2. During the luteal phase, PMDD/Dysphoric PMS participants showed significantly higher subcallosal-gyrus beta2 mean-Z activity than asymptomatic controls. Luteal subcallosal-gyrus beta2 abnormal-voxel values were descriptively higher in PMDD/Dysphoric PMS participants (19.43%) than in asymptomatic controls (4.13%); however, this voxel-percentage comparison is reported descriptively because luteal-phase between-group percentage-of-voxels analyses did not reach the study threshold for statistical significance. These findings support further investigation of DMN-linked neural activity, subcallosal-gyrus beta2 activity, and phase-related network adaptability in PMDD.

item.title: Neural Connectome Mapping of Chronotype in Young Adults: Associations with Neurotransmitter Profiles and Longitudinal Self-Control.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Chronotype is associated with self-regulation, but its functional connectivity correlates, neurotransmitter correspondence, and longitudinal associations with self-control remain unclear. We applied connectome-based predictive modeling (CPM) in a longitudinal cohort to identify resting-state connectivity features associated with chronotype. Cross-validated predictions showed a small correlation with reduced Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (rMEQ) scores in the discovery set (n = 816, r = 0.118, pperm = 0.007). A similar association was observed in validation set 1, a baseline hold-out sample from the same cohort (n = 681, r = 0.125, pperm < 0.001). Longitudinal evaluation used validation set 2, comprising two-year follow-up data from a subset of participants in validation set 1 (n = 594, r = 0.134, pperm < 0.001), providing a within-cohort assessment of whether the association was stable over time. Node-importance maps showed spatial correspondence with neurotransmitter maps. Both connectivity sets shared GABA-A and VAChT associations, with relatively receptor-weighted and transporter-weighted profiles in the positive and negative sets, respectively. In participants with complete two-wave data (n = 563), cross-lagged panel models indicated that baseline self-control was prospectively associated with higher positive-set strength (β = 0.256, p < 0.001) and lower negative-set strength (β = -0.228, p < 0.001); reverse paths were not significant. These findings provide evidence for chronotype-related functional connectivity features and their associations with neurotransmitter distributions and self-control in young adults. The validation and longitudinal evidence is limited to a single-site cohort, and cross-cohort generalizability remains to be established.

item.title: Static and dynamic intrinsic brain activity in eyes-closed and eyes-open resting-state conditions.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data are typically acquired under eyes-closed (EC) or eyes-open (EO) conditions, which are thought to reflect interoceptive and exteroceptive brain states. However, evidence for condition-dependent differences has largely relied on static analyses that provide limited information about temporal variability. Here, we investigated eye-state modulation of intrinsic brain activity by integrating multimetric static and dynamic analyses across multiple spatial scales. Static measures, including the amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF), fractional ALFF (fALFF), regional homogeneity (ReHo), and degree centrality (DC), were estimated to characterize low-frequency amplitude, relative spectral contribution, local synchronization, and network centrality. A sliding-window approach was used to calculate ALFF, fALFF, ReHo, and DC within successive windows, and their variability across windows was quantified. Static analyses revealed spatial differences between EC and EO across visual, sensorimotor, temporal, prefrontal, parietal, and subcortical regions. A particularly consistent finding across the static metrics was greater middle occipital gyrus involvement during EO. However, fALFF also showed an EC-related increase in the left calcarine cortex, indicating regionally heterogeneous effects within the occipital cortex. Dynamic analyses showed greater variability during EC in selected posterior visual regions, most consistently for dALFF and dReHo variability, whereas dfALFF and dDC variability were more sensitive to window length, mean adjustment, and spatial standardization. These findings demonstrate that eye state modulates intrinsic brain function through coordinated changes in both whole-scan measures and temporal variability across multiple spatial scales, highlighting the importance of jointly considering static and dynamic properties when investigating the neural organization of resting-state activity.

item.title: Differentiating language-specific from language-related network dynamics using dynamic functional connectivity analysis.
item.description:
Cognitive neurodynamics
Language processing is a highly complex dynamic neural activity that requires the recruitment of both regions critical for language processing and large-scale cognitive networks. Because language networks are interconnected and dynamically reconfigure their connections depending on task demand and complexity, it is challenging to differentiate language-specific networks form language-related cognitive networks during both resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) and task-based fMRI (tb-fMRI). Prior evidence demonstrated state-dependent differences in dynamic functional connectivity (FC) within identical networks across rest- and task-conditions. Based on this evidence, we hypothesized that examining dynamic FC patterns could help differentiate the functional specialization of large-scale neural networks in the human brain. Thus, we examined whether temporal patterns of dynamic FC could functionally differentiate networks engaged during a language task. Using a data-driven dynamic FC framework, we tested whether rest-task state transitions preferentially modulate subsets of large-scale networks. Specifically, we examined whether monotonic temporal trends in dynamic FC, used as a first-order approximation of sustained task engagement, were more prominent in networks showing task-sensitive dynamics, while others exhibited resting-state-like dynamics. We analyzed rs-fMRI and tb-fMRI data from 172 healthy participants (86 females, 27.6 ± 3.8 years old) from the Human Connectome Project. Dynamic FC analyses revealed significant state-dependent differences in correlation variability between rs-fMRI and tb-fMRI (Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.001). A subset of networks exhibited task-sensitive temporal modulation, whereas other networks showed dynamic patterns closely paralleled resting-like dynamics without reaching statistical significance. These findings suggest that dynamic FC provides a useful framework for functionally distinguishing language-specific networks from language-related cognitive networks. Supplementary information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11571-026-10579-0.

item.title: The unfolding symphony: unraveling brain dynamics via data-driven multi-scale functional connectivity in task-state fMRI.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Task-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) can characterize both regional responses and changes in statistical dependence among distributed brain systems. This narrative review examines dynamic and multiscale connectivity within a broader framework that distinguishes task-modulated functional connectivity, trial-wise covariation, effective connectivity, and data-driven state analysis. Sliding-window correlation, hidden Markov models, and co-activation patterns are compared by their data representations, temporal assumptions, and computational procedures; graph representations can be combined with each of these strategies. We discuss supervised recurrent, transformer, and graph models alongside unsupervised state discovery, self-supervised representation learning, and emerging brain foundation models. Explainability requires evaluation of model attributions, including graph masks and perturbation-based analyses, rather than anatomical plausibility alone. The spatial framework includes whole-brain networks, subnetworks, atlas-defined regions of interest, and voxel- or layer-level measurements. Proposed links across these levels remain hypotheses: faster sampling of the blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) signal does not directly resolve millisecond neural interactions, and resting-state or animal findings do not establish the corresponding mechanism during human tasks. Shared task-evoked responses, hemodynamic variability, motion, and analytical choices can all alter apparent connectivity. Progress therefore depends on matching the estimator to the scientific question, comparing against activation and static-connectivity baselines, and validating results across participants, sessions, and acquisition settings.

item.title: Replicable Connectivity and Spectral Alterations of Functional Networks in Major Depression
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is usually characterized in functional MRI through connectivity alone, often in samples too small to resolve its modest effects. Here we applied multi-scale, template-guided independent component analysis to resting-state data from the multi-site MDD-DIRECT cohort and jointly examined the connectivity, spectral content and spatial composition of 105 intrinsic brain networks. Differences between patients and controls were widespread, small and structured: cerebello-subcortical coupling was reduced, subcortical–somatomotor coupling was increased, and spectral power shifted from lower to higher frequencies, most prominently in the thalamus, which also showed the most altered connectivity. Spatial composition differed in every network examined. In a smaller independent cohort, the direction of effect agreed for 95% of significant connections, 78% of significant spectral effects and 77% of the largest spatial-composition effects. Depression therefore alters several distinct properties of intrinsic networks, consistently across cohorts and most prominently in the thalamus.

item.title: Excitation-inhibition imbalance in depression and the limits of observability: cohort-level inference from resting-state EEG with an amortised three-region Wilson-Cowan model
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Depression is widely thought to involve an imbalance between neuronal excitation and inhibition, but the idea has rarely been tested quantitatively at the level of macroscopic brain networks, because dynamical models are hard to fit to EEG spectra and fitting them person by person is prohibitively slow. We present a complete, reproducible pipeline that makes such a test possible, and we report where it succeeds and where it does not. Using eyes-closed resting-state EEG from 117 participants (22 with lifetime major depressive disorder, 95 without), we fitted a three-region excitatory-inhibitory network model with an amortised Bayesian method, in which a single shared library of simulations serves every participant and reduces inference to milliseconds per person. Depressed participants showed a consistent shift towards excitation in three core networks, together with a stronger inhibitory loop gain and a lower operating-point drive. The model's default-mode resonance frequency rose with symptom severity, whereas the conventional peak-frequency estimate computed from the same recordings did not. We then asked what the model actually buys. For distinguishing groups it did not outperform simple spectral measures, and its per-person low-frequency predictions were poor, so we restrict our claims accordingly. A real-time state observer detected sudden shifts in the network's operating point within milliseconds, yet could not reconstruct the moment-to-moment state, a limit set by the model's intrinsic randomness rather than by our algorithm. Finally, a dose-matched control showed that closed-loop stimulation is no more accurate than a fixed stimulus at the same dose, so we report the real-time feasibility of the loop without claiming an accuracy advantage. The contribution of the paper is therefore a reusable, calibrated inference pipeline together with an explicit map of its limits, including negative findings that we deliberately kept as results.
